messages.content: I want to go to whistler for skiing. Can you give me the 5 day forecast for both the top and bottom of the mountain.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve data. This function is commonly used for API calls and web scraping. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The Date Nager API provides access holiday information for over 100 countries, including the ability to query for long weekends. It leverages ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes to tailor the search to your specific region of interest. More information can be found in https://date.nager.at/Api

headers.description: Optional headers to send with the request as a dictionary of header values.

Content-Type.description: The media type of the resource being requested, typically 'application/json'.

Authorization.description: The credentials to authenticate a user agent with a server, typically formatted as 'Bearer {token}'.

timeout.description: The maximum amount of time to wait for a response from the server, in seconds. A longer timeout may be necessary for slower network connections or overloaded servers. This is a float type value.

params.description: URL parameters to append to the URL. Sent as a dictionary of key-value pairs.

query.description: The query parameter for search or filtering.

page.description: The page number parameter for pagination. Used to retrieve a specific page of results.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials formatted as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem), if required for the request.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names and values.

sessionid.description: Session identifier cookie, used to recognize client sessions on the server.

csrftoken.description: CSRF protection token cookie, used to prevent cross-site request forgery attacks.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary, mapping protocol or protocol and hostname to the URL of the proxy.

http.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTP requests, including the port number.

https.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTPS requests, including the port number.

stream.description: Whether to stream the download of the response. If False, the response content will be immediately downloaded. Streaming is useful for handling large files or responses.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not. Set to False to skip certificate verification, which is not recommended unless you are sure of the server's identity.

The user wants weather forecasts for Whistler ski area. They specifically ask for 5-day forecast for both the top and bottom of the mountain.

We need to provide them with relevant info. We have no direct tool for weather; we could call an external API like openweathermap but it's not listed among available tools. There's only one tool defined: `requests_get`. But that's generic; we might still use it to fetch data from some public weather API endpoint. However, there's no mention of allowed usage of arbitrary APIs. Usually we should avoid calling unknown endpoints due to policy restrictions? Let's check policies:

OpenAI policy says we cannot make real-time internet queries except via pre-defined tools. Here we do have a tool named `requests_get` that allows us to perform GET requests. That seems permissible. So we can attempt to get weather data using e.g., open-meteo.com or other free services. For example, open-meteo has a simple API: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=49.41&longitude=-122.78&hourly=temperature_2m etc. Or we can use WeatherAPI.com but requires API key. Another option: MetaWeather had been discontinued. There is also Visual Crossing Weather API requiring key. Maybe easiest: Use open-meteo because it's free and doesn't require auth. We'll just pass lat/lon coordinates for Whistler. Coordinates approximate: latitude ~48.75°N, longitude -123.7°W maybe? Actually Whistler Village at 50.1138°N, -121.9579°W? Wait let's confirm: Whistler Mountain base station near 50.112°, -121.958°. Top altitude about 1700 m above sea level. But location wise same lat lon. So we can treat top vs bottom difference minimal. But they asked separate forecast for top and bottom. Could differentiate by elevation effect? Might produce similar numbers though. Provide explanation that differences small.

But we can't guarantee accurate predictions without actual data. We can approximate using open-meteo's daily summary. Provide temperature ranges, precipitation probability, wind speed, snow depth perhaps. Also note that open-meteo returns hourly data; we can compute average for each day.

Let's plan: Use open-meteo API: 
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=50.12&longitude=-121.96&daily=weathercode,windspeed10min_max,precipitation_sum,snowfall_sum&timezone=AEST? Actually timezone param needed. Use timezone=America/Vancouver. Then parse JSON. Provide next five days starting tomorrow. Provide typical conditions.

However, we don't actually run code here. We can simulate expected output based on known patterns? Not possible. Instead we can explain how they'd obtain forecast themselves. But the question expects answer: "give me the 5 day forecast". Possibly we can respond with placeholder text referencing open-meteo API link where they can view details. But better to show sample forecast.

Given constraints, I think best approach: Provide general guidance plus sample forecast derived from open-meteo. Since we can't fetch live data now, we can illustrate what would happen if we called the API. But we can include instructions to call the API manually.

Alternatively, we can try to call the API ourselves within this environment. It's uncertain whether we have internet connectivity. According to guidelines, we can use the tool to fetch remote resources. So we can attempt to call open-meteo. Let's see if we can call the tool. I'll craft a request: 

```
{
   url:"https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
   params:{
      latitude:50.12,
      longitude:-121.96,
      daily:["weathercode","windspeed10m_max","precipitation_sum"],
      timezone:"America/Vancouver",
      start_date:"today", end_date:"...??" 
   }
}
```

But open-meteo uses start_date & end_date optional. Without specifying, defaults to today onward until max 30 days ahead. So we can simply specify daily fields. Let's test quickly mentally: Suppose we call the API. Response includes dates array and arrays for each variable. We then interpret first 5 entries after today's date. Provide temperatures? Actually open-meteo does not return temperature directly in daily mode unless we add "temperature_2m_min"/max. Add those too. And snowfall sum. So our params: daily=["temperature_2m_min","temperature_2m_max","snowfall_sum","precipitation_probability_mean"] maybe. But open-meteo supports "precipitation_probability_mean"? Yes. So we can gather all.

Thus we can produce forecast table: Day | Min Temp | Max Temp | Precip Prob | Snowfall Sum | Wind Speed Max.

Now we need to differentiate between top and bottom. We can say that top is higher altitude (~1600m). Temperature tends to drop ~6°C per km. At 1500m difference relative to valley (~200m?), so roughly 8°C cooler. So adjust min/max accordingly. Similarly precipitation chance slightly lower/higher? Harder. Provide estimate: subtract 8°C from temps. Keep other variables same.
